questions.q: In event-driven architecture, what is a producer's relationship to its consumers?
options: The producer calls each consumer directly and waits for every one of them to confirm processing
The producer announces an event without knowing how many consumers exist or what they do with it afterward
A producer can only ever have exactly one consumer
The producer and consumer must be the same system for the architecture to count as event-driven
questions.explain: The defining decoupling of EDA is that the producer raises an event without direct knowledge of, or dependency on, how many consumers are subscribed or what each one does with the event.

questions.q: What is the main architectural benefit this lesson attributes to decoupling producers from consumers?
options: It guarantees every consumer processes an event at exactly the same instant
It eliminates the possibility of any consumer ever missing an event
It removes the need for an event bus entirely
A new consumer can start reacting to an existing event without the producer's logic being modified at all
questions.explain: Because producers don't know about consumers, a new consumer can subscribe to an already-existing event and start reacting to it without any change to the producer's logic — the architectural flexibility that is EDA's main value.

questions.q: What does the existence of Salesforce's High-Volume Platform Events add-on signal to an architect, per this lesson?
options: That serious event-driven designs can outgrow the base per-edition Platform Event allocation, and sizing event volume against the org's actual allocation is part of the architect's job
That Platform Events have no practical volume limit at all on any edition
That Platform Events are being deprecated in favor of REST callouts
That the add-on is required for every Salesforce org regardless of event volume
questions.explain: The add-on exists specifically because base per-edition Platform Event allocations can be outgrown by real production event-driven designs — an architect is expected to check the current allocation for the org's edition rather than assume a number, and plan for the add-on if volume requires it.

questions.q: What does "eventual consistency" mean in the context of event-driven architecture?
options: Every consumer is guaranteed to process an event within exactly one second
Only one consumer out of many will ever actually receive the event
All consumers will eventually reflect a given event, but not necessarily all at the same instant
Consistency is never achieved in an event-driven design
questions.explain: Eventual consistency means every consumer will come to reflect the event's effect over time, but there's no guarantee they all do so simultaneously — one consumer might react in milliseconds, another after catching up from a brief outage.

questions.q: For which kind of business process does this lesson say eventual consistency is a genuine limitation rather than an acceptable trade-off?
options: Cross-system analytics that doesn't require split-second alignment
A business process that needs every system looking at exactly the same data right now
Sending a notification to an unrelated system
Logging an event for later audit review
questions.explain: Eventual consistency is a real limitation specifically for processes that need every system aligned on the same data at the same instant — for most notification, analytics, or loosely-coupled synchronization use cases, the delay is an acceptable, often invisible, cost.
